paragraphs: A brain-computer interface can change on both sides of its feedback loop. Its decoder learns how to interpret the user's neural signals, while feedback lets the user adapt the neural activity producing those signals. The paper models these coupled changes rather than treating decoder learning as an isolated process.

The authors express this interaction as a multi-agent version of linear quadratic Gaussian control. In this formulation, neural encoding and decoding are both participants in an optimization process. Simulations characterize how decoding improves as the two adapt, producing patterns that qualitatively resemble previously demonstrated improvements in closed-loop experiments.

The framework also motivates a modified decoder update that accounts for the encoder changing at the same time. This update improves simulated co-adaptation dynamics. The contribution is therefore both an explanatory model and a proposed adjustment to learning: recognizing that the user is adapting can change how the decoder should update. Its benefits for practical user learning remain a promising application of the modeling results.
neurips-2013-a-multi-agent-control-frame.tldr: Modeling users and decoders as jointly adapting agents suggests a decoder update that improves simulated brain-computer interface learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies kernel regression when the relevant structure of the input space is unknown. Its central concern is local adaptation: the procedure should respond to the properties of the space and the regression function around the particular point where a prediction is needed.

Two unknown quantities matter together. Local metric dimension describes the dimensional structure near a point, while local Hölder continuity describes how smoothly the regression function varies there. The result establishes adaptation to both quantities at once. This matters because adapting to the geometry alone would leave the function's local behavior unaddressed, and adapting only to smoothness would leave the geometry unaddressed.

The guarantee holds with high probability simultaneously across all points in the metric space. That simultaneous statement gives the result broader scope than a guarantee established only for one preselected location. The authors identify this as the first kernel-regression result combining both forms of local adaptation, without requiring the metric space's structure to be known.
neurips-2013-adaptivity-to-local-smoothn.tldr: Kernel regression can adapt simultaneously to unknown local dimension and local smoothness, with a high-probability guarantee across the metric space.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning problems can be approached by solving a linear program and then rounding its solution into the form the original problem requires. This paper targets the computational work in that first stage. It develops an efficient approximate solver intended to support applications that use this rounding strategy.

The method uses a quadratic-program relaxation to make large linear programs accessible to parallel stochastic coordinate descent. This connects the linear-programming task to an optimization procedure that can distribute work across coordinates. The aim is to obtain useful approximate solutions efficiently while retaining guarantees about computation time and solution quality.

The authors supply a new perturbation analysis for a quadratic-penalty formulation of linear programming, together with a convergence result. These theoretical ingredients support the running-time and quality guarantees. In the reported comparison, their software is an order of magnitude faster than Cplex and produces similar solution quality. The finding supports approximate optimization as a practical route for the LP-rounding problems considered.
neurips-2013-an-approximate-efficient-lp.tldr: A quadratic relaxation enables parallel approximate LP solving, with theoretical guarantees and reported speed gains over Cplex at similar solution quality.

paragraphs: State-space models describe changing systems through underlying states and the rules governing their evolution. This paper develops a fully Bayesian approach for nonlinear models whose transition dynamics are not restricted to a fixed parametric form. A Gaussian process prior supplies the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamical behavior.

The main inference choice is to integrate out the transition dynamics and work directly with the joint smoothing distribution, which represents uncertainty about the underlying sequence of states given the observations. Specially designed particle Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers approximate this distribution. This organizes inference around state trajectories while accounting for uncertainty in the dynamics.

After approximating the smoothing distribution, the method can express the predictive distribution for state transitions analytically. Sparse Gaussian process models further reduce computational complexity. Together, these choices connect flexible modeling, Bayesian uncertainty, and more efficient computation: the approach learns about hidden state sequences without requiring the dynamics to be explicitly retained throughout the inference procedure.
neurips-2013-bayesian-inference-and-lear.tldr: Particle MCMC and marginalized Gaussian process dynamics enable Bayesian inference in flexible nonlinear state-space models.

paragraphs: Conditional random fields predict several related response variables together, using an undirected graph to represent their dependencies given input covariates. Familiar versions accommodate some response types well, but are less suited to others, including counts. The paper develops a broader construction that starts from distributions appropriate for individual response variables.

Each response's conditional distribution, given the other responses and the covariates, is required to belong to a univariate exponential family. This leads to multivariate conditional models based on distributions such as Poisson, negative binomial, and exponential. The construction also addresses how to specify the feature functions that express interactions between responses and covariates.

For learning, the authors develop tractable penalized estimators and a unified analysis of sparse structure recovery. They show that exact recovery of the graph can be achieved with high probability. The contribution links model construction and estimation: the same framework expands the available response distributions and supplies a theoretical basis for learning which dependencies are present.
neurips-2013-conditional-random-fields-v.tldr: Building CRFs from univariate exponential-family conditionals expands supported response types and enables high-probability structure-recovery guarantees.

paragraphs: Smell requires inferring which odors are present from activity distributed across receptor neurons. The paper develops neural implementations of two approximate inference algorithms that could perform this task: one uses a variational approach, and the other uses sampling. Both address how a network could separate the underlying odors from their combined receptor responses.

A central modeling choice is a spike-and-slab prior over odor concentrations. It assigns zero concentration to most odors, expressing the assumption that most possible odors are absent. After translating the algorithms into neural dynamics, the authors find that both identify correct odors in less than 100 milliseconds, while eliminating false positives takes roughly 500 milliseconds.

Those similar time courses lead to similar behavioral predictions, but the models differ in connectivity, neural computations, and predicted activity. The authors therefore propose that experiments could distinguish them at the neural level. Such a distinction could illuminate both the mechanisms of odor inference and the different ways neural networks might represent uncertainty.
neurips-2013-demixing-odors-fast-inferen.tldr: Two neural odor-inference models predict similar recognition timing but different neural activity, offering a possible way to distinguish their coding strategies.

paragraphs: LASSO estimates coefficients from noisy linear observations using a penalty that encourages sparse solutions. Choosing that penalty depends on knowing how much error the estimate contains and how noisy the observations are. This paper develops estimators for both the coefficient-estimation error measured in the ℓ2 norm and the noise variance.

The approach combines Stein's unbiased risk estimation with results connecting approximate message passing to LASSO risk. The authors establish consistency as problem dimensions increase for design matrices with independent Gaussian entries. They also extend validity to a broader class of Gaussian designs, but that extension depends on a conjecture from statistical physics.

These estimators can support optimal selection of the regularization parameter. The authors describe their risk estimator as the first asymptotically consistent one in this setting, and simulations show their variance estimator outperforming several existing methods. The distinction between established and conditional results matters: the independent-Gaussian guarantee is proved, while the broader-design claim retains its stated conjectural dependence.
neurips-2013-estimating-lasso-risk-and-n.tldr: New LASSO error and noise estimators support regularization selection, with consistency proved for independent Gaussian designs.

paragraphs: The paper examines stochastic learning and optimization when sparsity is a property of the observed data. It identifies a tradeoff: sparse observations can require more samples for accurate learning, yet their structure can also make computation more amenable to parallel and asynchronous execution. Both effects belong in an assessment of sparse-data methods.

The authors derive matching upper and lower bounds on minimax rates. These bounds characterize the best worst-case performance available in the studied setting, and the paper supplies algorithms that attain those rates. The algorithms are adaptive, achieving the best possible rate for the data actually observed.

The computational contribution builds on the same sparsity structure. The authors construct parallel and asynchronous algorithms that retain minimax optimality, so the benefits of those execution styles are compatible with the statistical guarantees. Experiments on medium- to large-scale learning tasks complement the theory. The result connects the extra information needed for sparse-data learning with opportunities to organize its computation more efficiently.
neurips-2013-estimation-optimization-and.tldr: Sparse data can increase sample requirements while enabling adaptive, parallel, and asynchronous algorithms that attain optimal minimax rates.

paragraphs: Some observations contain several meaningful levels of organization. In calcium imaging, pixels relate to neurons, and neurons relate to assemblies. The paper develops a matrix decomposition that reflects this layered structure by expressing observations as a product of more than two sparse matrices, with rank decreasing toward higher levels.

The method learns relationships between levels and permits both hierarchical and heterarchical organization. This allows the representation to capture more than a prescribed hierarchy. Its optimization scheme adjusts all levels jointly, so the interpretation at one level can be learned together with the relationships and representations at the others.

The proposed bilevel sparse heterarchical matrix factorization simultaneously represents constituent neurons, their assembly memberships, and the activity time courses of neurons and assemblies. Experiments fully recover the structure of difficult synthetic data designed to resemble experimental observations. On real calcium imaging data, the method produces plausible interpretations. These findings support the representation's usefulness while distinguishing demonstrated synthetic recovery from the plausibility of its real-data interpretations.
neurips-2013-learning-multi-level-sparse.tldr: Jointly learned sparse matrix layers reveal neurons, assemblies, and their activity, recovering synthetic structure and producing plausible calcium-imaging interpretations.

paragraphs: The paper studies low-rank matrix factorization with a discrete restriction: every entry in one factor must be either zero or one. Motivated by computational biology, this setting combines the nonconvexity of matrix factorization with a large combinatorial search space. For dimension m and rank r, that factor has 2^(m·r) possible binary configurations.

The authors give an algorithm that provably recovers the underlying factorization in the exact case. Its worst-case operation count is O(mr2^r + mnr). The exponential term therefore depends on the rank rather than on the product of rank and data dimension, a substantial change from the size of the full configuration space.

The proof draws on combinatorial theory centered on the Littlewood-Offord lemma. This is the key bridge between a seemingly prohibitive discrete constraint and a more manageable recovery procedure. The guarantee concerns exact factorization, and its operation count still includes exponential dependence on rank. Within that scope, the result establishes that searching all possible binary factors is unnecessary.
neurips-2013-matrix-factorization-with-b.tldr: A combinatorial algorithm provably recovers exact binary-component factorizations with exponential dependence on rank rather than the full binary factor size.

paragraphs: The paper introduces online probing, a prediction problem in which information has a price. On each round, a learner chooses which feature values to buy and predicts using those observations. It then has the option to pay to observe the loss against which its prediction is evaluated.

The learner's total cost includes both prediction imperfections and purchased information. This creates linked decisions about what to observe before predicting and whether to acquire feedback afterward. Buying more information may help learning, but the purchase itself contributes to the objective the learner is trying to control.

The authors analyze two variants distinguished by whether labels are available for free. They provide algorithms and upper and lower regret bounds for each, and show that charging for labels significantly increases regret. The result makes the cost of feedback a central part of the learning problem: access to the information used to evaluate predictions can materially affect attainable performance, alongside the cost of observing features.
neurips-2013-online-learning-with-costly.tldr: Online probing jointly prices features, feedback, and prediction errors, and its regret bounds show a substantial penalty when labels also cost money.

paragraphs: The paper connects two families of approximate reinforcement-learning methods: greedy value-function approaches and value-based policy-gradient approaches. It shows that optimistic policy iteration can encompass most of the former as well as natural actor-critic methods. An important subset of policy-gradient methods appears as a limiting case within this broader formulation.

The resulting continuum allows direct interpolation between these approaches. Its interpretation concerns how strongly the Markov assumption enters policy improvement. The authors relate this, in spirit, to the continuum supplied by TD(λ) methods for policy evaluation, giving a common perspective on algorithms often placed in separate categories.

A second result identifies a significant tradeoff for a substantial subset of soft-greedy value-function methods. Although these methods can potentially avoid policy oscillation and chattering, they cannot converge to an optimal policy except in a specified pathological case. In approximate settings, the authors therefore suggest that many greedy methods face either unstable policy changes or systematic suboptimality. The impossibility claim applies to the analyzed subset.
neurips-2013-optimistic-policy-iteration.tldr: Optimistic policy iteration unifies major reinforcement-learning approaches, while a substantial soft-greedy subset faces a qualified impossibility of optimal convergence.

paragraphs: Perceptron models and spiking variants such as the Tempotron offer powerful accounts of learning, but connecting their rules to biological synapses remains a challenge. This paper asks whether realistic changes in synaptic strength, combined with neuronal dynamics, can implement those learning capabilities in networks of spiking neurons.

The authors prove a sufficient combination for realizing the original Perceptron Learning Rule. It uses anti-Hebbian spike-timing-dependent plasticity at excitatory synapses and Hebbian-shaped plasticity at inhibitory synapses, acting together with hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic neurons. They also show that these dynamics efficiently learn Tempotrons.

The mechanism could support learning mappings between spatiotemporal activity patterns in different brain regions and could contribute to long-term cortical memories. Those biological roles are proposed possibilities. The established computational result is that the specified interaction of plasticity and neuronal dynamics can realize the learning rule. Its broader lesson is that synaptic plasticity must be considered together with the behavior of the neurons participating in learning.
neurips-2013-perfect-associative-learnin.tldr: Specific excitatory and inhibitory timing-dependent plasticity mechanisms, combined with neuronal hyperpolarization, suffice to implement perceptron learning.

paragraphs: Combining individually learnable stochastic processes can produce a mixture that is harder to learn, or fails to remain learnable under the same definition. The paper studies this difficulty for dependent data, using a notion of learnability in which generalization error approaches zero in probability for concept classes of finite VC dimension.

The authors propose defining predictive PAC guarantees by conditioning on the mixture component responsible for the sample path, rather than on past observations. This changes the reference point for evaluating prediction. Their argument is that component-conditioned guarantees better reflect a realistic learner's demands and avoid several serious difficulties arising from dependence.

Under this definition, they establish a PAC generalization bound for mixtures whose error is no worse than that of each component. The guarantee is tied to the proposed conditioning choice; it does not erase the initial difficulty for arbitrary definitions of mixture learning. The paper also characterizes mixtures of absolutely regular, or β-mixing, processes, adding a structural result about dependent processes.
neurips-2013-predictive-pac-learning-and.tldr: Conditioning predictive PAC guarantees on a process's mixture component yields bounds that preserve component-level generalization performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maintain the data structures used by partition-based regression when training examples arrive sequentially. A useful streaming procedure must keep updating its representation as more data arrives while preserving predictive accuracy. The challenge therefore involves both the work needed for each update and the statistical quality of the resulting regression.

The authors prove that the structure can be maintained in O(log n) time at step n. At the same time, the procedure achieves a nearly optimal regression rate of approximately n^(-2/(2+d)), with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here d is the unknown metric dimension, so the accuracy statement is expressed in terms of geometry that need not be known beforehand.

The paper also proves a regression lower bound that is independent of a specified data size. This makes the benchmark more appropriate for a continuing stream, where the amount of available data keeps changing. Together, the results connect efficient ongoing maintenance with a nearly optimal statistical rate in that setting.
neurips-2013-regression-tree-tuning-in-a.tldr: Streaming partition-based regression can achieve logarithmic update time and a nearly optimal error rate governed by unknown metric dimension.

paragraphs: Visual training and test data often differ because of lighting, pose, backgrounds, resolution, and other conditions. Domain adaptation addresses these mismatches, but it commonly assumes that data has already been divided into domains. Treating each dataset as one domain can miss the distributional differences within and across collections.

The paper proposes discovering latent domains automatically in image and video data. Its formulation combines distinctiveness with learnability. Identified groups should have different underlying distributions, while each group should also support learning a strong discriminative model. This makes the grouping task sensitive to both distributional separation and its usefulness for recognition.

The authors introduce a nonparametric representation and an efficient optimization procedure for distinctiveness, coupled with the learnability constraint. The approach can discover domains among training and test data and is extensively evaluated on object and human activity recognition. Its contribution is a way to construct the domains adaptation methods need, using the visual data's structure instead of relying solely on dataset boundaries.
neurips-2013-reshaping-visual-datasets-f.tldr: Automatically discovering visually distinct yet learnable domains provides a more meaningful basis for adaptation than dataset boundaries alone.

paragraphs: Logistic-normal topic models can discover how latent topics are correlated, but fitting them is computationally difficult. The logistic-normal prior and multinomial topic proportions do not form a conjugate pairing, which complicates inference. Existing approaches either impose restrictive mean-field assumptions or struggle to scale to large applications.

The paper develops a partially collapsed Gibbs sampler using data augmentation. This introduces auxiliary quantities into the inference procedure to address the computational difficulty. The sampler approaches the provably correct distribution, giving the method a distributional justification beyond simply producing a convenient approximation for the model.

A parallel implementation improves time efficiency and supports learning correlations among thousands of topics from millions of documents. Extensive empirical results demonstrate the approach's promise. The contribution joins two requirements that are especially relevant here: inference that targets the correct distribution and an implementation that can handle large collections. This enables the correlation structure offered by logistic-normal topic models to be explored at a substantially larger scale.
neurips-2013-scalable-inference-for-logi.tldr: An augmented Gibbs sampler with a parallel implementation scales logistic-normal topic inference to millions of documents and thousands of correlated topics.

paragraphs: Cauchy random projections are commonly used to work with ℓ1 distances in high-dimensional data. This paper asks what can be obtained by retaining only the sign of each projected value. That choice produces a much simpler representation, making the relationship between those signs and useful data similarities the central question.

The authors show that the probability of two projected signs differing can be accurately approximated as a function of chi-square similarity. This similarity is useful for nonnegative features, including histograms encountered in text and vision. The result links a very compact projection outcome to a comparison measure already relevant for these data types.

Experiments indicate that sign Cauchy projections are promising for large-scale learning. The authors also extend the idea to sign α-stable random projections and derive a bound on the corresponding collision probability. The main chi-square connection is an accurate approximation, while the broader projection family receives a probability bound; these are distinct forms of support for the approach.
neurips-2013-sign-cauchy-projections-and.tldr: Signs of Cauchy projections provide a compact representation whose disagreement probability closely tracks chi-square similarity for nonnegative data.

paragraphs: A Markov chain describes a system using initial-state probabilities and probabilities of moving between states. This paper tackles the inverse problem of inferring those probabilities from observations available at only a limited set of states. The observations include how often states are visited and rates of reaching one state from another.

City traffic provides a motivating application: a monitoring system may need to infer volumes across an entire road network while measuring only a small number of locations. The paper formulates the general inference task as regularized optimization over probability functions. It uses natural-gradient optimization to solve that formulation efficiently.

Evaluation on synthetic and real-world datasets, including city traffic monitoring data, demonstrates the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a computational route from limited observations to an inferred model of system-wide transitions. By optimizing the probabilities that define the chain, the method addresses the missing model directly and connects measurements at observed states to estimates for the larger dynamical system.
neurips-2013-solving-inverse-problem-of-.tldr: Regularized natural-gradient optimization infers Markov-chain probabilities from limited state observations, with demonstrations including city traffic data.

paragraphs: The paper investigates Langevin Monte Carlo on the probability simplex, the space of nonnegative probability vectors whose entries sum to one. This setting matters for inference involving distributions over categories: the quantities being estimated must remain meaningful probabilities. The work focuses on developing a sampling method for that space.

The proposed method is stochastic gradient Riemannian Langevin dynamics. The authors describe it as simple to implement and suitable for online use. Online applicability is a central part of the contribution, connecting a method for probability-valued quantities with a setting in which inference proceeds as data becomes available.

The paper applies the method to latent Dirichlet allocation in an online setting. In that application, it demonstrates substantial performance improvements over the state-of-the-art online variational Bayesian methods considered. This supplies empirical support for the proposed sampling approach in topic modeling. The stated result concerns that online LDA comparison, while the methodological contribution is the development of Langevin dynamics for the probability simplex.
neurips-2013-stochastic-gradient-riemann.tldr: An online Langevin sampling method for probability vectors substantially improves performance over the compared online variational methods in latent Dirichlet allocation.

paragraphs: Graphical-model structure learning often assumes that the process generating the observations remains unchanged throughout the data. Real systems can instead change without an explicit signal. The paper addresses environments that are locally stationary: the generating model is stable over local periods but need not stay the same globally.

The authors introduce LoSST, a heuristic algorithm that tracks changes in graphical structure or model parameters dynamically and in real time. This extends the learning objective beyond finding one fixed model. The method is intended to follow evolving dependencies and parameter values as the process generating the observations changes.

Simulations compare LoSST with batch-mode learning under both stable and changing generating structures. It performs comparably when the structure is globally stationary and significantly better when it is only locally stationary. These results support the value of tracking changes in the tested dynamic settings. Because LoSST is presented as a heuristic and the findings come from simulations, the evidence is empirical rather than a universal performance guarantee.
neurips-2013-tracking-time-varying-graph.tldr: LoSST tracks changing graphical models in real time and outperforms batch learning in simulations with locally stationary structure.

paragraphs: Recognizing novel categories is difficult when they have few labeled examples or none at all. This paper combines transfer learning with semi-supervised learning so that unlabeled examples of those categories also contribute. Its Propagated Semantic Transfer method links knowledge about established categories with the organization of the new data.

The approach has three ingredients. External semantic knowledge, including linguistic or expert information, connects known and novel categories. A graph-based learning algorithm then exploits the manifold structure of novel classes in zero-shot and few-shot settings. Finally, object- or attribute-based intermediate representations improve local graph neighborhoods compared with using raw features.

The authors evaluate the approach on Animals with Attributes and ImageNet for image classification, and MPII Composites for activity recognition. It consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art transfer and semi-supervised methods across these datasets. The findings support using semantic relationships and unlabeled-data structure together: semantic information enables transfer, while the graph lets the available novel examples shape how that information is propagated.
neurips-2013-transfer-learning-in-a-tran.tldr: Propagated Semantic Transfer combines semantic knowledge and graphs of unlabeled examples to improve zero-shot and few-shot recognition on three datasets.

paragraphs: Stochastic And-Or grammars represent both how parts compose larger structures and how those structures can take alternative forms. They have been used for data such as images and events. The paper develops a unified formalization that does not depend on which type of data is being modeled.

The authors also propose an unsupervised procedure for learning both a grammar's structure and its parameters. Starting from a trivial grammar, the method repeatedly introduces compositions and reconfigurations through a unified process. It optimizes the grammar's posterior probability, allowing the organization of the model itself to be learned alongside its probabilistic quantities.

Empirical evaluations apply the approach to event grammars and image grammars, obtaining performance comparable to or better than previous approaches. These results support the usefulness of one learning framework across both applications. The main contribution is the combination of a shared formalism with structural learning: the method can build richer grammatical organization from a simple starting point rather than requiring that organization to be specified in advance.
neurips-2013-unsupervised-structure-lear.tldr: A unified unsupervised method learns And-Or grammar structure and parameters, with comparable or better results on image and event grammars.

paragraphs: An overcomplete topic model can contain more latent topics than observed vocabulary words. Such models are not identifiable in general: observations may fail to distinguish the underlying representation uniquely. This paper establishes conditions under which observable moments of a suitable order can nevertheless identify the model.

The results give generic identifiability under a topic-persistence constraint. Sufficient conditions involve higher-order expansion properties of the topic-word matrix or population structure, including a perfect matching between latent topics and higher-order observed words. The authors also show that random structured topic models satisfy identifiability with high probability in the overcomplete regime.

The framework permits general nondegenerate distributions over topic proportions and can therefore accommodate arbitrarily correlated topics. Its implications extend to tensor decomposition: the results establish uniqueness for a structured-sparse class within Tucker decompositions that is more general than CP decomposition. The contribution is a set of sufficient structural conditions for identifiability, connecting recoverable overcomplete topic models with uniqueness of their associated tensor representations.
neurips-2013-when-are-overcomplete-topic.tldr: Topic persistence and higher-order structural conditions can make overcomplete topic models generically identifiable, even with arbitrarily correlated topics.

paragraphs: The paper develops an image-recognition model that can identify categories with no training images, using knowledge about those categories from unsupervised text corpora. It also handles mixtures of familiar and unseen categories. This matters because a recognition system may need to decide whether an image belongs to an established class before predicting a novel one.

The model treats word distributions in text as a semantic space and learns to map images near the word vectors for their classes. It requires no manually defined semantic or visual features for words or images. The resulting image embeddings help distinguish seen from unseen categories, after which separate recognition models can be used.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on classes with thousands of training images alongside reasonable performance on unseen classes. Two strategies emphasize different outcomes: one attains high accuracy on unseen categories, while the other makes conservative novelty predictions to preserve accuracy on familiar categories. The contribution therefore includes both cross-modal knowledge transfer and strategies for balancing recognition across seen and unseen classes.
neurips-2013-zero-shot-learning-through-.tldr: Mapping images into a text-derived semantic space enables recognition of unseen classes while supporting strong performance on familiar categories.
